w12.001: The Physical Dimensions (and Mass) of the Master Universe
w12.002: Appendix XVI, Physical Space (and Mass) Magnitudes of the Master Universe (pp. 381–388)
w12.003: The Urantia Book never states the size of the master universe outright, yet here and there it leaves distances and masses that can serve as starting points for a calculation. Sadler gathers these clues and uses them to estimate the dimensions of the grand universe and of the four outer space levels. His key assumption is that each space level, moving outward, is a steady hundred times wider than the one within it. When the results are translated into everyday objects, from a tennis ball to a sphere larger than the moon, one gains a felt sense of how differently scaled are the arena in which the Supreme Being emerges and the arena in which God the Ultimate emerges.
w12.004: 1. The Raw Data: Distance and Mass (orig. pp. 381–383)
w12.005: Sadler begins by collecting what the text says about distance and mass. For distance his point of departure is Orvonton. According to the revelators, the outermost inhabited systems lie a little under two hundred fifty thousand light-years from the headquarters of the superuniverse [32:2.11]. Sadler treats this figure as the radius of the superuniverse and therefore puts its "transverse diameter," the span crossing it from outer rim to inner rim, at roughly 500,000 light-years. Beyond it lies a quiet belt.
w12.007: Farther out, force activity grows steadily stronger over a stretch of more than twenty-five million light-years. Supposing that the intensity falls away again as far as it rose, Sadler judges the first outer level to be about fifty million light-years across. The text adds that, more than fifty million light-years beyond that, activity has been detected which heralds a second outer space level [12:1.15].
w12.008: The data on mass reveal how heavy outer space already is. Because of the dark gravity bodies that encircle it, Havona outweighs all seven superuniverses together [12:1.10]. Even so, most of the pull of Paradise gravity is spent on holding matter beyond the grand universe.
w12.011: Sadler assumes that all seventy thousand of these aggregations belong to the Primary Space Level, forming the great cluster that contains the 375 million new galaxies our telescopes will one day reach [12:2.3]. Were they in the second level, those galaxies could never become visible to us.
w12.012: 2. How Large Is the Grand Universe? (orig. pp. 383–384)
w12.013: In principle, the grand universe's radius should be Havona's radius with a superuniverse's transverse diameter added to it. Here Sadler meets two obstacles. Measuring all the way to the center of things would carry the calculation past the inner boundary of space, and Paradise does not exist in space. Moreover, the Urantia Book gives no dimensions at all for the central universe.
w12.014: His solution is to leave Havona out. Havona's billion worlds are set in seven orderly circuits and presumably use their space economically. Orvonton, by contrast, must make room not only for a trillion inhabited worlds but for countless suns and satellites and turbulent, swirling nebulae. If Orvonton were merely a thousand times the size of Havona, the radius of Havona would amount to just one-tenth of one per cent of Orvonton's transverse diameter. Even if this guess were off, the error would vanish beside the enormous numbers soon to appear.
w12.015: Sadler therefore sets the diameter of the grand universe at about a million light-years and its radius at about half a million. To handle the large figures that follow, he then fixes a scale. Let the radius of the grand universe be one inch (about 2.5 centimeters); the grand universe becomes a ball two inches across, roughly a slightly undersized tennis ball.
w12.016: 3. The Four Outer Space Levels (orig. pp. 384–387)
w12.017: The Primary Space Level: A Tennis Ball in a Room
w12.018: Set the grand universe's radius of 500,000 light-years beside the first level's transverse diameter of 50 million, and the ratio is one to a hundred. On the tennis-ball scale that becomes one inch against a hundred inches (about 2.5 meters). The radius of the grand universe and first level combined is then 101 inches, the diameter 202 inches, close to sixteen feet (about 5 meters). Sadler invites the reader to picture a high-ceilinged living room some five meters in length, breadth, and height, with a single tennis ball floating at its very center. How many such balls would that room hold?
w12.019: He supports the picture with further clues. Ten Master Architects serve the grand universe, but seventy serve the Primary Space Level. And the seventy thousand aggregations of matter, though still at an early stage, already command ninety-five per cent of Paradise gravity; as they mature, that share will rise above ninety-nine per cent.
w12.020: The Secondary Space Level: A Cube the Size of a City Block
w12.021: From here on, the text supplies no sizes. That the space levels grow larger outward is clear, but whether the rate of growth holds steady or accelerates cannot be known. Sadler takes the more cautious option and assumes it holds steady. One to a hundred then continues as a hundred to ten thousand, giving the second level a transverse diameter of about 800 feet (250 meters) and an overall diameter of some 1,600 feet (500 meters). Sadler likens this to a long city block, stands the block up as a cube, hangs the living room at its center, and places the tennis ball in the middle of the room.
w12.022: The Tertiary and Quartan Levels: A City and the Moon
w12.023: Applying the same ratio once more, the third level's transverse diameter comes to 80,000 feet, which Sadler rounds conveniently to sixteen miles (about 25 kilometers), with an overall diameter of thirty-two miles (about 50 kilometers). One may imagine a three-dimensional city fifty kilometers long, wide, and high. The last, the Quartan Space Level, is 1,600 miles across, and the whole master universe about 3,200 miles (some 5,000 kilometers) in diameter. Take the moon, roughly 2,100 miles in diameter, enlarge it by about half, and the size is right.
w12.024: Sadler checks the effect of ignoring the inner levels. Adding together one inch, eight feet, and 808 feet merely puts about a fifth of a mile on top of sixteen miles; measured as a diameter, the total stays under thirty-three miles. That is only a little over one per cent of 3,200 miles, so the approximation is roughly ninety-nine per cent accurate.
w12.025: Sadler's scale model: each space level is a hundred times wider than the one before (sizes in the figure are not proportional)
w12.026: 4. The Scale at a Glance (orig. pp. 387–388)
w12.027: Transverse-diameter ratios of the space levels and Sadler's scale model (metric conversions by the commentators)

w12.031: A city-block cube 500 m on each side

w12.035: Every figure in this appendix rests on two assumptions. First, the fifty-million-light-year width of the Primary Space Level comes from a symmetry argument: force intensity declines over the same distance through which it rose, twenty-five million light-years. Second, from the Secondary level outward, a constant hundredfold increase in width determines everything. The text affirms neither. Still, Sadler chose the more conservative course; if the ratio in fact grows, the real master universe will be far larger than this. Converted into light-years, his assumptions give the Quartan level a transverse diameter of fifty trillion light-years (our conversion).
w12.036: For the most part, the Urantia Book tells the story of the grand universe during the second universe age. Sadler closes the appendix on this note: the experiential emergence of Supremacy is a function of the grand universe, whereas the emergence of Ultimacy requires all of that plus the development of the four outer space levels. A single tennis ball and a single sphere larger than the moon: such is the difference between the arenas in which these two Deities emerge.
w12.037: The size of Havona is unknown, but it is judged small compared with a superuniverse and is left out of the calculation. The grand universe is about a million light-years in diameter.
w12.038: The Primary Space Level is roughly fifty million light-years across, a hundred times the radius of the grand universe.
w12.039: Since the text gives no figures beyond the first level, Sadler adopts the conservative assumption of a steady hundredfold increase in width.
w12.040: In the scale model the grand universe is a tennis ball, the Primary level a living room, the Secondary a city block, the Tertiary a cubic city, and the Quartan a sphere larger than the moon.
w12.041: The emergence of Supremacy is the work of the grand universe; the emergence of Ultimacy is the work of the entire master universe.
w12.042: The Time Dimensions of the Master Universe
w12.043: Appendix XVII, Time Magnitudes of the Master Universe (pp. 389–396)
w12.044: The text offers even less on time than on space, yet Sadler builds a series of calculations on a handful of dates and registry numbers. He first works out the age of an Abandonter, a very ancient native of Uversa; from that he derives the age of Orvonton, and from that again the length of the entire second universe age. Finally he transfers the spatial ratio of the previous appendix to time in order to estimate the length of the ages of outer space. To cope with such huge numbers he devises a new yardstick, the "Andronover Time Unit."
w12.045: 1. The Age of a Native of Uversa (orig. pp. 389–390)
w12.046: The first subject Sadler chooses is the Abandonter. The Urantia Book introduces the Abandonters as permanent citizens of the Uversa headquarters sphere, created by the representatives of the Ancients of Days together with the Seven Reflective Spirits [37:9.12]. Their age is not given. Sadler reaches it by way of Lucifer.
w12.047: He begins with the age of the Lanonandek Sons, Lucifer's order. Michael began organizing Nebadon about four hundred billion years ago [119:0.7], and the Lanonandeks were created as a group sometime afterward. The oldest inhabited worlds of Nebadon, meanwhile, go back two hundred billion years [57:3.10], and the Lanonandeks, as System Sovereigns and Planetary Princes, would have had to be at work before any inhabited world existed. Their age must therefore lie between four hundred and two hundred billion years. Sadler picks the midpoint, three hundred billion.
w12.048: Next comes the relativity of time.
w12.050: Sadler reads this passage as a proportion: three days in the life of Lucifer correspond to two and a half seconds in the life of a native of Uversa. Three days contain 259,200 seconds; divided by 2.5, that yields 103,680. Multiplying three hundred billion years by 103,680 gives the age of the Abandonter: 31,104 trillion years, or about thirty quadrillion in round numbers. Since the Andronover nebula was born 987 billion years ago, a little under a trillion years [57:1.3], this Abandonter is some thirty thousand times older than Andronover.
w12.052: Paper 54:5.13 compares "two or three days" with "two and a half seconds," and the comparison arises from an illustration setting the lifetime of a mortal beside the lifetime of Lucifer. Sadler chose "three days" for his calculation, and he reinterpreted the lapse of time "from the viewpoint of Uversa" as the lifetime of an individual Uversa native. Nothing indicates that the text intended such a computation. The figures in this appendix are best received, from beginning to end, as plausible approximations.
w12.054: Just as Nebadon is older than the Lanonandeks, its oldest natives, so Orvonton should be older than the Abandonters. By how much? Sadler again answers with a proportion. If Andronover is taken to be about a trillion years old, the first sixty per cent of that span, up to Michael's arrival four hundred billion years ago, was devoted wholly to physical development. Dating the history of Nebadon from Michael's arrival, the local universe is about a hundred billion years, that is, one-third, older than Lucifer. Applying the same ratio, Orvonton is the Abandonter's thirty quadrillion years plus ten quadrillion more, or about forty quadrillion years.
w12.055: 3. The Length of the Second Universe Age (orig. pp. 391–395)
w12.056: Percentages That Show How Far We Have Come
w12.057: If Orvonton is already forty quadrillion years old, how long is the whole second age, counting from the time the Ancients of Days were created until the superuniverses are settled in light and life? Sadler computes several percentages that indicate how much of the course has already been run. About seven trillion inhabitable worlds are planned for the grand universe [15:2.9], and Urantia's registry number reads as follows.
w12.059: Dividing this number by seven trillion gives about seventy-six per cent. At the time Urantia was registered, then, human life had already appeared on somewhat more than three-fourths of the planned worlds. Sadler works through other numbers in the same way.
w12.060: Sadler's percentages (the denominators 100,000 and 700,000 are his assumptions)
w12.064: Number of Salvington's tertiary circuit supervisor [24:1.11]
w12.065: Number of secondary circuit supervisors on Uversa [24:1.9]
w12.069: The values cluster between seventy-six and eighty-seven per cent. Sadler also weighs the differences. Even if the Michaels were created in numbered sequence, there is no assurance they were assigned in that same order, so the eighty-two per cent of the tertiary circuit supervisors may better reflect the proportion of local universes in operation, and this agrees nicely with the eighty-one per cent of the census directors. Alternatively, the seventh superuniverse alone may be lagging behind.
w12.071: Between the commissioning of a local universe and its settling in light and life lies an immense distance. That is why Sadler makes the proportion of inhabited worlds his most important indicator.
w12.073: If a single world fails to be settled, its local universe cannot be settled; if a single local universe is unsettled, the superuniverse cannot be. Rounding seventy-six per cent down to seventy-five, Sadler concludes that three-fourths of the second age has passed. In that case one-third must be added to Orvonton's forty quadrillion years to obtain the length of the whole age. He trims the additional thirteen quadrillion or so to ten, and estimates the full second universe age at about fifty quadrillion years, fifty thousand times the age of Andronover.

w12.075: 4. The Duration of the Outer Space Ages (orig. pp. 395–396)
w12.076: If the second age lasts fifty quadrillion years, how long will the ages be in which the outer space levels grow? Sadler simply carries the spatial ratio over to time: if each space level is a hundred times wider, the age of its growth should be a hundred times longer. The age of the Quartan Space Level then comes to a hundred million times the second age, a number of years written as a five followed by twenty-four zeros. Using such figures is as awkward as measuring astronomical distances in miles.
w12.077: So Sadler creates a unit of time analogous to the light-year. He takes as one unit the longest period treated in the Urantia Book, the age of Andronover, just under a trillion years, and names it the "Andronover Time Unit" (ATU).
w12.078: Lengths of the universe ages in Andronover Time Units (Sadler's estimates)
w12.085: The outer space levels will need an extraordinarily long time to mature, but they are correspondingly vast.
w12.087: Each number in this appendix is stacked on the assumptions before it: the choice of a midpoint for the age of the Lanonandeks, the three-day benchmark, the rounding to seventy-five per cent, the premise that time is proportional to spatial width. Hence "fifty quadrillion years" or "five trillion ATU" is not an answer but a gauge of orders of magnitude. Sadler himself offers it as little more than something better than an uncalculated guess. Even so, such a gauge lets one feel how early a dawn our present age is within the whole history of the master universe.
w12.088: Sadler estimates the age of the Lanonandeks at three hundred billion years and, deriving a ratio of 1 to 103,680 from the time illustration in 54:5.13, calculates the age of an Abandonter at about thirty quadrillion years.
w12.089: Applying the ratio by which a local universe is one-third older than its Lanonandeks, he puts the age of Orvonton at about forty quadrillion years.
w12.090: Because a superuniverse is settled only when all its inhabited worlds are settled, he treats the seventy-six per cent (about three-fourths) of inhabited worlds as the most important indicator.
w12.091: On that basis he estimates the entire second universe age at about fifty quadrillion years, fifty thousand times the age of Andronover.
w12.092: Transferring the spatial ratio to time, each outer space age is a hundred times longer than the last, the sixth reaching five trillion ATU.
w12.093: All these figures are approximations built on assumptions and should be read as a gauge of orders of magnitude.
w12.094: God the Ultimate and His Nature
w12.095: Appendix XVIII, The Nature of God the Ultimate (pp. 397–414)
w12.096: Among the experiential Deities, God the Ultimate is the second. Whereas God the Supreme emerges with the completion of the grand universe, God the Ultimate emerges only when the whole master universe is finished, including the four outer space levels. Sadler divides this emergence into seven stages, examines the nature and attributes of Ultimacy and its relations to various beings, and makes clear that the "Ultimacy of Deity" is not a being but a level on which Deity functions. It is an appendix in which the statements of the text are few and Sadler's inferences many.
w12.097: 1. Three Experiential Deities and Three Scales (orig. p. 397)
w12.098: The Foreword places God the Supreme, God the Ultimate, and God the Absolute on the first, second, and third levels of unifying Deity expression.
w12.100: Sadler suggests that if the space and time required for the emergence of Supremacy are represented by "1," then by the reckoning of the two preceding appendices the emergence of Ultimacy may be symbolized by "100 million" and that of God the Absolute by "infinity." The emergence of God the Absolute will lie beyond the master universe, perhaps bound up with an unlimited Cosmos Infinite.
w12.101: 2. The Emergence of Ultimacy: Seven Stages (orig. pp. 398–403)
w12.103: Ultimacy is not Deity eternal in the past. It is eternal in the future but had a beginning in time.
w12.105: The Supreme emerges in three stages: as a spirit person in Havona, in the present power-personality synthesis, and in the future completed evolution. Sadler reasons that the growth of Ultimacy, which spans five universe ages and five space levels, should involve more stages, and he proposes seven. His grounds are that both the sovereignty of a Creator Son and the personalization of a Creative Spirit unfold through several stages.
w12.106: Seven stages in the emergence of Ultimacy and the universe ages (the staging is Sadler's proposal)
w12.107: Initial Emergence in Havona and Present Activity
w12.108: Because the transcendental precedes the finite in historical order, Sadler infers that Ultimacy appeared in Havona at the same time as Supremacy or even earlier. The presence in Havona is plainly stated by the text.
w12.110: Sadler conjectures that even in the "quiet time" before the superuniverses, unrevealed absonite realities in Havona may have been modified in keeping with the purposes of the Ultimate. In the present second age, the Ultimate is still a reality in the process of "becoming," yet already active. Part of the unpredictability of emerging energies may be explained by His activity [12:6.6], and ascending mortals become conscious of Him as they enter the Corps of the Finality.
w12.112: Sadler acknowledges, however, that while something is known of the mechanism of the power-personality synthesis of the Supreme, nothing at all is known of the corresponding mechanism of the Ultimate.
w12.114: When the superuniverses are complete and the Supreme has emerged, He will govern those creations while the Ultimate exercises overcontrol [118:2.4], and the first experiential Trinity, of which the Supreme is a member, can actually be formed. Sadler expects that Ultimacy will enter this "post-Supreme" stage when the Primary Space Level opens.
w12.115: The next three stages lie in territory where the text is silent. Sadler surmises that the sovereignty of the Ultimate will grow by one step as each outer space level is completed, and he names these Primary, Secondary, and Tertiary Sovereignty. This layering has no counterpart in the growth of Supremacy, which is completed within a single space level. At each stage a further personalization (perhaps superpersonalization) of Ultimacy would occur, much as a Creative Spirit becomes increasingly personal while her local universe grows.
w12.117: The final stage comes when growth reaches the Quartan Space Level and the entire master universe is finished. At that time the first experiential Trinity also becomes fully unified. Because the master universe is subinfinite and quantitatively limited, this goal is attainable. The achievement of this twofold goal, a completed universe and a unified Trinity, is the emergence of God the Ultimate.
w12.119: Besides the unification of the Trinity, the success of the post-Havona members of God the Sevenfold and the experiential functioning of Ultimacy itself also play their part in this emergence. Drawing on what is said of the Supreme, Sadler infers that the emerged Ultimate will become the actual sovereign of the master universe and will confront its citizens with God the Absolute as their next challenge.
w12.120: 3. The Nature of Ultimate Deity (orig. pp. 403–407)
w12.121: Deity Flanked on Both Sides by Trinities
w12.122: God the Supreme is evolutionary-experiential, God the Ultimate transcendental-experiential, and God the Absolute existential-experiential. Sadler points out that the Ultimate alone stands between two experiential Trinities: He emerges through the unification of the first and at once becomes a member of the second. It is here that Sadler looks for the reason the Foreword calls the Ultimate a "self-projected" Deity.

w12.126: Sadler examines these phases one at a time. The "personally experiencible" phase would point to the (super)personality of the Ultimate, which other personalities and superpersonalities may someday contact. The "control directing" phase is the power aspect within Ultimacy, just as the Supreme has the Almighty Supreme, and the text supplies its name.
w12.128: The "tensionally unifying" phase may be the activity by which Ultimate Mind binds the Omnipotent to God the Ultimate, as Supreme Mind binds the Almighty Supreme to God the Supreme. The "unrevealed aspects" signal that the nature of the Ultimate is far more complex than that of the Supreme. Sadler concludes that the personality of the Ultimate is inseparable from the nonpersonal phases of His Deity.
w12.129: Power-personality synthesis in Supremacy and Ultimacy compared (the mechanism on the Ultimate's side is Sadler's analogy)
w12.131: The text says very little about ultimate mind.
w12.133: By analogy with Supreme Mind, Sadler conjectures that Ultimate Mind, too, will be bestowed by the Infinite Spirit when the synthesis begins, and that the Seven Master Spirits and Majeston will serve as its reservoir and point of convergence. On spirit there are a few more clues.
w12.135: From this Sadler concludes that the Ultimate possesses spirit He can bestow upon creatures, and that the "supernal absonity" possessed by the Master Architects [31:9.1] must likewise be found in the Ultimate. He also understands the Ultimate as superpersonal, while stressing that because the prepersonal, the personal, and the superpersonal are interconnected [0:5.4], personalities too can make contact with Him.
w12.136: 4. The Attributes of God the Ultimate (orig. pp. 408–409)
w12.137: The most distinctive attribute of Ultimacy is the transcendence of time and space. The finite is bound by time and space; the absolute is timeless and spaceless; the absonite is related to both but bound by neither.
w12.139: The Foreword portrays the Ultimate as omnipotent, omniscient, and omnipresent Deity [0:1.10]. Sadler reads each of these three attributes together with its limits.
w12.141: Omniscience is a foreknowledge arising from the transcendence of time, yet it does not diminish the free will of creatures. Omnipresence arises from the transcendence of space, and the space presence of the Ultimate extends to the very edge of the master universe.
w12.143: 5. Relation to the Paradise Deities and the Master Universe (orig. pp. 409–410)
w12.144: Just as the Supreme in some measure represents the Paradise Trinity on the finite level, the Ultimate represents the Trinity in a qualified sense on the absonite level. When we try to picture the Trinity as a single person we think of God the Supreme; the transcendentalers, in the same way, think of God the Ultimate [10:8.2]. The three Paradise Deities now co-operate with the Ultimate not personally but as the Trinity [10:7.3]. Sadler speculates that this relationship will change once the experiential Deities leave their prepersonal era. Outside Havona the presence of the Father is limited by the Supreme and conditioned by the Ultimate [3:2.15].
w12.145: With respect to the master universe, the Ultimate stands midway between the Absolutes and the Supreme. The appearance of the master universe depends on the Absolutes for its potential, on the Ultimate for its direction, and on the Supreme for its evolutionary co-ordination [12:6.9–11]. Sadler interprets this to mean that the Ultimate "creatively organizes" the potentials of the three Absolutes in advance, so that the creators of the subabsolute level are able to transmute them.
w12.147: In Sadler's own terms, the experiential story of the master universe as a whole, embracing creation, evolution, and eventuation, is in large part the story of the Supreme and the Ultimate.
w12.148: 6. The Transcendentalers and Other Beings (orig. pp. 411–413)
w12.149: Sadler considers five groups connected with the Ultimate. The Transcendentalers, who are neither creators nor creatures but "⟦Q 30:1.92⟧eventuators⟦/Q⟧" [30:1.92]; the Master Architects, their governing corps; and the master force organizers, who work under the Architects' jurisdiction, will all be subject to God the Ultimate. The fourth group are the Personalized Adjusters, who act as executives of the Architects of the Master Universe and perform the unexpected in the transcendental domains of God the Ultimate [109:7.3].
w12.151: The fifth group are the Qualified Vicegerents of the Ultimate, whose existence alone the text reports [106:4.3]. Just as the Unqualified Supervisors of the Supreme represent only God the Supreme [55:12.4], Sadler reasons by analogy that these vicegerents represent God the Ultimate, serving as advisers before His sovereignty is established and as superadministrators afterward. The contrast between "unqualified" and "qualified" in their titles hints that the representation provided by the latter is in some way incomplete.
w12.153: The "Ultimacy of Deity" is the name neither of a single Deity nor of a single being, nor even of a single Trinity. It is a level of reality on which one phase of Total Deity is active: the seventh, "ultimate" level. Sadler identifies three realities that occupy it: the Trinity of Ultimacy, that is, the Paradise Trinity as it functions with respect to the absonite level; the experiential Trinity Ultimate, which co-ordinates the master universe; and God the Ultimate, who emerges from that Trinity's unification. Their interaction appears as providence on the transcendental level. Providence is an "overcontrol other than personal" extending from God the Sevenfold by way of the Almighty up to the Ultimacy of Deity itself [118:10.4].
w12.154: Supremacy serves the grand universe in a finite way; Ultimacy serves the master universe in an absonite way.
w12.157: The division of the Ultimate's emergence into seven stages, and in particular the stages of Primary, Secondary, and Tertiary Sovereignty, is Sadler's proposal and not something the text states. Even concerning the stages of a Creator Son's sovereignty, which he cites in support, the text speaks cautiously of "six, perhaps seven" stages [21:3.4]. In addition, the passage Sadler cites as the source of "supernal absonity" (31:9.5) is actually 31:9.1.
w12.158: God the Ultimate, second of the experiential Deities, emerges, on the second level of unifying Deity manifestation, with the completion of the entire master universe.
w12.159: Sadler proposes seven stages for the emergence of Ultimacy: initial emergence, pre-Supreme, post-Supreme, Primary, Secondary, and Tertiary Sovereignty, and completed emergence. The three middle stages are inference without textual basis.
w12.160: The emerged Ultimate has phases that are control directing, personally experiencible, and tensionally unifying, along with unrevealed phases; the phase of control is called "the Omnipotent."
w12.161: The Ultimate's attributes of omnipotence, omniscience, and omnipresence all derive from the transcendence of time and space, and they do not extend to the nondoable or the unknowable.
w12.162: The appearance of the master universe depends on the Absolutes for potential, on the Ultimate for direction, and on the Supreme for evolutionary co-ordination.
w12.163: The Ultimacy of Deity is not a being but the seventh functional level of Total Deity.
w12.165: Appendix XIX, The Second Experiential Trinity (pp. 415–427)
w12.166: When the master universe is complete and God the Ultimate has achieved final power-personalization, the second experiential Trinity, the Trinity Absolute, can actually be formed. Its members are God the Supreme, God the Ultimate, and the unrevealed Consummator of Universe Destiny. To solve the problem of the Supreme being present in three Trinities at once, Sadler sketches the growth of the Supreme in seven stages. He then compares the three Trinities and reasons that because the goal of the Trinity Absolute is infinite, it will never be fully unified, yet it may attain the absolute in quality, if not in quantity.
w12.167: 1. The Formation of Two Experiential Trinities (orig. pp. 415–416)
w12.168: At the dawn of eternity, two subabsolute levels of existence were projected by the Paradise Trinity. Sadler takes these to be the finite and the absonite levels.
w12.170: Since Deity seeks unification on every supermaterial level, and Trinity function always embraces Deity reality, two levels must give rise to two experiential Trinities. The first, the Trinity Ultimate, consists of the Supreme Being, the Supreme Creator Personalities, and the Architects of the Master Universe; it will actually form at the end of the second age, unify the master universe, and as a result God the Ultimate will emerge. When the Ultimate finally emerges at the end of the sixth age, the second experiential Trinity can be formed.
w12.172: A Trinity is not a union of three persons but of three Deity realities. The Supreme and the Ultimate belong to it as Deity, while as persons they exist apart from the Trinity. The Consummator of Universe Destiny, of whom almost nothing is known, adds great uncertainty to the future of this Trinity.
w12.173: 2. Deity Present in More Than One Trinity (orig. pp. 417–418)
w12.174: The Trinity Absolute raises a new problem. The Deity of the Supreme is present in the Trinity Ultimate, in the Trinity Absolute, and at the Trinity of Trinities' second level, and the Ultimate is present in two of these. Sadler elects to call that second level the "third experiential Trinity."
w12.175: Does the Supreme then have three Deity natures, or one nature present three times? Sadler holds that the Supreme is one Deity whose presence will function on absonite, coabsolute, and coinfinite levels. If the existential Father can be contacted on every level from the finite to the absolute, he argues, there is no reason God the Supreme should not grow upward through comparable experiential levels. The text designates the three relationships by different terms.
w12.177: Sadler reads the difference among these three terms to mean that the Supreme continues to grow in a "postpersonal" era even after His full emergence.
w12.178: 3. The Growth of the Supreme (orig. pp. 419–421)

w12.196: 5. The Growth of the Experiential Trinities (orig. pp. 422–424)
w12.197: Sadler draws the theme of this section from a single sentence.
w12.199: Both experiential Trinities pass through at least three stages: "qualified reality" at inception, "factual reality" at formation, and "unified reality" at destiny. The Trinity Ultimate is at present a qualified reality. Only the corps of Master Architects exists in full; the corps of Supreme Creators still lacks the Universe Sons and Spirits not yet commissioned. At the end of the second age it forms as a factual reality, goes on "becoming unified" while the outer space levels are completed, and at the end of the sixth age becomes a unified reality.
w12.200: The Trinity Absolute follows the same path through the first two stages. It may be a qualified reality even now, and it forms as a factual reality when the sixth age closes. The third stage, however, is where the road is blocked. Its goal is absolute, so its unbounded reach toward final unification collides with the hard fact of infinity. Sadler calls this "The Barrier of Infinity," or alternatively "The Impasse of the Absolutes."
w12.201: 6. A Trinity That Is Never Unified (orig. pp. 424–427)
w12.203: The text says that the function of the Trinity Absolute suggests a stage far larger than the master universe [106:6.2]. If an unlimited Cosmos Infinite lies beyond the master universe, then the full functioning and unification of this Trinity would mean the absolute actualization of all potentials [106:6.3]. That would amount to exhausting the three Absolutes of potentiality, the triunity of potential. Yet the text declares:
w12.205: Only the infinite Paradise Trinity can override infinity. The two experiential Trinities are composed of derived Deities and are not infinite [0:12.3]. Still, the text also says that the Trinity Absolute is "absolute in total function," and here Sadler sees a first way out.
w12.207: Absoluteness of quality and absoluteness of quantity can be separated. The Trinity Absolute may be limited in scope yet function absolutely in value. Accordingly, Sadler concludes that this Trinity will activate the three Absolutes in a limited but ever-widening manner, and that the experientializing of the Deity Absolute will go on forever without ever being completed. The personalization of God the Absolute through the unification of the Trinity will be frustrated.
w12.208: The Consummator of Universe Destiny: An Open Door

w12.212: 7. The Function of the Trinity Absolute (orig. p. 427)

w12.221: Distinguishing quantity from quality, Sadler reasons that the Trinity Absolute will be limited in quantity yet function absolutely in quality.
w13.003: If the eras after the Supreme Being appears are called the post-supreme ages, then the time after God the Ultimate has emerged and the master universe stands complete deserves the name post-ultimate age. Is it then a seventh universe age, or a "post-universe" age lying beyond the finished master universe? Sadler leaves the question open, allowing that this era may close the earlier series while also opening a new one.

w13.023: 2. The Completed Master Universe and Beyond (orig. pp. 430–432)
w13.025: By the reckoning of Appendix XVI, if the grand universe is taken as one unit, the master universe comes to roughly one hundred million. The size defeats the imagination, yet the master universe still has an outer limit, and eternity is long. Sooner or later that limit must be reached, and with it the Ultimate Adventure comes to a close.
w13.026: At that point God the Ultimate will be co-ordinating the entire master creation, together with the two Trinities, on the level of the ultimacy of Deity, while the Supreme Being will still be sovereign over the inner universes. Sadler pictures our own planet as having gone well past the seventh stage of light and life into some ultimate status. The revelation does speak of the persistence of such worlds.
w13.028: Completion and commencement: a "nuclear" master universe
w13.029: For Sadler the completed master universe is at once an ending and a beginning. He names five developments that carry it from the static state of fulfilled destiny into the dynamic state of seeking a new one.
w13.030: **The Supreme Being**: His growth as mind potential and as Almighty Supreme is finished, but His relationship to the "third level of Deity manifestation" may not be. Sadler reads this as a coabsolute relationship to be formed within the Trinity Absolute.
w13.031: **God the Ultimate**: He passes beyond His prepersonal phase into a phase of continuing growth, and He too arrives at coabsolute status.
w13.032: **The Trinity Absolute**: It can take shape only after the Ultimate has emerged, so its formation begins early in this age.
w13.033: **The Supreme-Ultimate**: This dual Deity association, which the revelation speaks of as a future union, is expected to appear at the opening of the age.
w13.034: **God the Absolute**: The third experiential Deity becomes a fresh challenge to the citizens of the finished master universe. After the Supreme Adventure and the Ultimate Adventure comes the Absolute Adventure.
w13.035: Sadler holds that the second experiential Trinity will work outward, beyond the master universe, rather than within it. The revelation likewise hints that its function reaches past the master creation.
w13.037: In other words, the finished master universe becomes a new "nuclear universe" for the Cosmos Infinite that will form around it. Havona was once the nucleus of the superuniverses; now the entire master universe becomes a nucleus surrounded by a far larger cytoplasm.
w13.038: 3. Creatures of Time Adjusting to Eternity (orig. p. 433)
w13.039: Here Sadler turns to the human story. We are creatures of time, yet as we mature we gradually work free of confinement to the present moment. Our decisions draw more deeply on the past and look further toward their consequences. After survival this span widens beyond comparison. A trillion years of life would bring one to the present age of the Andronover nebula, and by Sadler's arithmetic, when the sixth age ends, we will be five trillion times older than Andronover.
w13.040: Thought Adjuster fusion adds a further dimension.
w13.042: Sadler's calculation runs as follows. Suppose that the past-eternity memory the Adjuster brings is taken in gradually, in step with our own growth. After a trillion years of living, absorbing another trillion years' worth of such memory gives a remembered past of two trillion years; if foresight extends equally far, the temporal base becomes four trillion years. One would then be grasping time four times faster than time actually elapses, a sure advance in the quantitative understanding of eternity. A qualitative sense of eternity, Sadler adds, arises when one crosses over to Paradise from Havona's innermost circuit.
w13.043: 4. Changes in the Potential for Growth (orig. pp. 434–436)

w13.067: The Idea of a Cosmos Infinite
w13.068: Appendix XXI, The Concept of the Cosmos Infinite (pp. 437–444)
w13.069: The Urantia Book teaches that space extends past the outer edge of the master universe. Sadler calls the boundless creation that will one day unfold out there the Cosmos Infinite, and he first shows that the idea has a footing in the text. He then examines how it might begin, how it can be reconciled with finite space, what its natives will lack, and the thought that Havona is already prepared for it.
w13.070: 1. The Textual Basis of the Concept (orig. pp. 437–438)
w13.071: The cosmic map of The Urantia Book is simple. Paradise lies at the center, Havona surrounds it, and the seven superuniverses in turn surround Havona. Together these form the grand universe; add the four outer space levels and the whole is the master universe. Space, however, stretches still further.
w13.073: Sadler sees that farther space as the site of a future endless universe. Havona, the first universe, stands at the center as eternity's creation; the last universe would lie at the periphery as infinity's creation. If Havona embodies the idea of existential perfection, the Cosmos Infinite embodies the idea of existential-experiential perfection.
w13.074: Sadler insists that this is no idle fancy and gathers passages to support it. The most direct concerns the triunity of energy infinity.
w13.076: The revelation also says that the Architects of the Master Universe recognize a relationship to something greater [106:7.7], describes the coabsolute level as a field of "supermaster universe" expression [106:0.7], and reports the view that full expression of the Infinite requires an infinite stage.
w13.078: On this foundation Sadler posits an endless creation encircling the entire master universe. It has an inner edge but no outer boundary, a beginning but no completion. Its ever-larger concentric zones will each fulfill their destiny, but the Cosmos Infinite as a whole will never be finished.
w13.079: The text's cosmos-infinite and Sadler's Cosmos Infinite
w13.080: In The Urantia Book the lowercase, hyphenated word cosmos-infinite is less the name of one particular creation than a tentative way of pointing to the unbounded cosmos beyond the master universe (106:6.3). Sadler capitalizes it as Cosmos Infinite and makes it the proper name of a final universe. This book uses Sadler's form when speaking of his concept and the text's form when quoting the revelation; the idea that it is a single, defined creation should be remembered as Sadler's interpretation.
w13.081: 2. The Beginning of the Cosmos Infinite (orig. p. 439)
w13.082: Havona appeared together with the Infinite Spirit. Following this analogy, Sadler suggests that the Cosmos Infinite might first appear when the Supreme and the Ultimate trinitize God the Absolute. There is a difference, though. Havona appeared all at once and in its entirety, whereas the Cosmos Infinite would merely make its first appearance. Havona is a fixed quantity; the Cosmos Infinite is not.
w13.083: The Supreme Being and God the Ultimate respectively embrace all evolved physical power and all transcendental physical power. Sadler imagines that when the two join in an act of trinitization, the material level too will resound, and the "inner zone" of the peripheral domain of infinity might suddenly materialize.
w13.084: Even that inner zone would be almost beyond conceiving. Sadler suggests it might exceed the master universe by as great a factor as the master universe exceeds the grand universe. And it would be the smallest region of the Cosmos Infinite.
w13.085: Sadler's picture of the Cosmos Infinite: an "inner zone" around the master universe and a boundary that keeps moving outward
w13.086: 3. Finite Space and an Infinite Universe (orig. pp. 439–441)
w13.087: A real difficulty arises here, for the revelation states clearly that space is not infinite.
w13.089: It also says that the quiet zones of midspace eventually enclose all space [11:7.3]. If space is the container of motion, resistance to motion should mount near its edge, leaving no room for creative activity. How can a universe without limit fit inside a space that has limits?
w13.090: Sadler weighs three possibilities for the volume of space. If the volume were constant, space would be a finite quantity, which sits poorly with the text's description of it as absolutely ultimate.
w13.092: A shrinking volume would not suit an expanding creation. That leaves only the idea that the volume of space is increasing. The revelation says that space is a bestowal of Paradise and seems to originate just below nether Paradise [11:2.11]; Sadler reads in the word "originate" a process still going on.
w13.093: If space is a constantly growing quantity, it has an outer boundary at any given moment, but at the next moment that boundary lies further out. The boundary has a location only in time, never in eternity. As long as space grows faster than creation, it can never confine a potentially infinite universe. Sadler finds this idea compatible with space respiration [11:6.4]: the alternating in-breath and out-breath of space are like waves rising and falling on a tide that steadily advances. This is Sadler's inference, built by joining several pieces of textual data; the revelation itself does not teach that space is expanding.
w13.094: 4. The Needs of the Cytoplasm Enlarge the Function of the Nucleus (orig. pp. 441–442)
w13.095: Sadler revisits the principle from Appendix XI that the needs of an outer universe enlarge the function of an inner one. In giving, Havona moves beyond its original limitation as a merely perfect universe.
w13.096: The principle repeats itself three times over.
w13.097: The chain of ministry that supplies what is lacking (Sadler's summary)
w13.099: Paradise and Havona beings → superuniverse ascenders
w13.100: Beings from the grand universe → citizens of outer space
w13.101: Citizens of the completed master universe → natives of the Cosmos Infinite
w13.102: The natives of the Cosmos Infinite will begin their existence on some coabsolute level from the very start, without any finite or absonite experience at all.
w13.103: Sadler admits that such words carry almost no meaning for us, yet he says the principle can be "felt" in the life of Jesus. Just as a perfect One came among imperfect humans and shared divine perfection with them, so we will one day share what we have with the citizens of the outer universes, and in a still more distant future, together with them, with the natives of the Cosmos Infinite.
w13.105: Sadler sets the last universe beside the first. Because Havona has always existed, its original plan must already have anticipated the future requirements of the Cosmos Infinite. He pairs passages from the text with his own inferences; the pairings can be summarized as follows.

w13.112: Sadler rounds off the comparison in the language of thesis and synthesis. Havona stands as an existential thesis, one of absolute perfection, put forth by the Universal Father and the Eternal Son and completed by the appearance of the Conjoint Actor. By contrast, the Cosmos Infinite would be an experiential thesis, one of coabsolute perfection, which the Supreme and the Ultimate put forth and which is set in motion by the trinitization of God the Absolute. The first and the last interlock in the same pattern.
w13.113: The revelation says that space reaches beyond the master universe and refers tentatively to a cosmos-infinite; Sadler develops this into a final creation he calls the Cosmos Infinite.
w13.114: The Cosmos Infinite has an inner edge but no outer boundary, a beginning but no completion.
w13.115: Sadler conjectures that its "inner zone" may appear when the Supreme and the Ultimate trinitize God the Absolute.
w13.116: The hypothesis of increasing spatial volume, offered to reconcile finite space with an infinite universe, is Sadler's inference, not a teaching of the text.
w13.117: Citizens of an earlier universe pass on what they possess to the citizens of a later one, and Havona was designed from the first with that final universe in view.
w13.120: The Urantia Book repeatedly says that the experiential Deities "power-personalize." Sadler treats this as a basic law of master universe growth and analyzes it. His answer is that in eternity God did not synthesize all actual reality into one, but left that task to the experiential Deities. The synthesis takes place on three levels, finite, absonite, and absolute; it is achieved on the first two but can never be completed on the absolute level.
w13.121: 1. What the Words Mean: Personality and Power (orig. pp. 445–447)
w13.122: Power-personality synthesis is the process of uniting power and personality. But what exactly is being united with what? Because the revelation gives both "power" and "personality" meanings that differ from the dictionary, the words must be clarified first.
w13.123: On personality, the text offers description rather than definition. Personality is an unsolved mystery and a revelation of God; God is personality and is will. Below the absolute level, personality is relatively free of antecedent causation; it has no identity of its own, yet it unifies the identity of a living energy system. From this Sadler concludes that personality is distinct from the three energies of spirit, mind, and matter. Those energies can be expressed in both quality and quantity, but personality can be expressed only in quality.
w13.124: Sadler's analogy is the color red. No one has ever beheld redness in isolation; what we see is always a red thing. Personality likewise never appears in isolation; we always know someone. Yet as redness wholly determines the color of an object, personality pervades and governs the entire being in which it is found.
w13.125: On power, the text speaks in connection with the Supreme.
w13.127: In the physical realm, "universe power" refers to the stage at which energy has come under intelligent control. Sadler supposes that mind and spirit have comparable stages of maturity, and he reserves the fullest sense of the word power for the three energies as governed by the Supreme Creators and integrated in the Almighty. In short, power-personality synthesis means uniting organized energy (physical, mental, and spiritual) with personality.
w13.128: 2. Why the Synthesis Takes Place (orig. pp. 447–451)
w13.129: In search of an answer Sadler goes back into the eternal past and sets two narratives side by side: the story of the actual and the story of the potential.
w13.131: The starting point is the absolute unity of God's nature. When the Father expressed Himself in the Original Son, the Isle of Paradise appeared as a kind of counterpart, and actual reality divided into the personal and spiritual Son and the nonpersonal, nonspiritual Paradise. Even so, on Paradise spirit energy and monota are distinguished only by name; they are one. This is a sign that the two were originally a single reality.
w13.132: Tension arises between reality diverging in these two directions, and the Father and the Son act together; the Infinite Spirit and the central universe appear. The Infinite Spirit is the source of mind, and mind co-ordinates matter and spirit. What Sadler stresses is what did not happen at this point. The Conjoint Actor co-ordinates the Son and Paradise but does not synthesize them. Rather than binding all actual reality into one, God establishes thesis after thesis of Deity. The Father is the prior thesis, the Son the unqualified thesis, the Spirit the conjoint thesis, and the Trinity the undivided thesis. Thesis is laid upon thesis; the tension is not resolved but actually increases. Paradise remains alone.
w13.134: The narrative on the side of potentiality begins in the same way. The Father's presence beyond Havona is hidden in the potentials of infinity, held on the Deity side by the Deity Absolute and on the non-Deity side by the Unqualified Absolute, two exactly opposite expressions. But here the stories part. On the potential side the two are perfectly unified.
w13.136: The story of the actual and the story of the potential: the potential side is synthesized in the Universal Absolute, while the actual side reaches only the co-ordination of mind, and Paradise stands alone
w13.137: Sadler's conclusion is this. What took place on the actual side was not a synthesis of all actual reality but the unification of all actual Deity reality, namely the Paradise Trinity. The task of unifying the whole of actual reality was handed on to the experiential Deities: God the Supreme, God the Ultimate, and God the Absolute. That, he holds, is the eternal background for the challenge, after Havona, of synthesizing power and personality. The interpretation is an original inference of Sadler's, woven together from many statements in the text.
w13.138: 3. The Challenge of Synthesis and Its Three Levels (orig. pp. 452–454)
w13.139: According to Sadler, a final completion of the revelation of God would require that the Unqualified Absolute be wholly materialized in an infinite creation, that the Deity Absolute fully emerge as God the Absolute, an "experiential absolute person," and that the two be completely unified experientially. This is beyond thought. Existentially the three Absolutes are already one in the Universal Absolute, but to realize that unity experientially would take another eternity.
w13.140: What is impossible on the absolute level is possible on subabsolute levels: first the whole of the finite is power-personalized, and then the whole of the absonite. Why exactly three levels? According to the text, the Paradise Trinity is actually existential, while its potentials are all experiential [0:12.2]. In relation to the finite the Trinity functions as the Trinity of Supremacy, in relation to the absonite as the Trinity of Ultimacy, and absolutely as Total Deity. Hence there are three experiential Deities.
w13.142: Sadler sees this as a kind of chain reaction. Because the experiential Deities were latent in the Trinity, they must become factual; because experiential Deities evolve, experiential Trinities must appear. All divine activity on the finite level is power-personalized in God the Supreme and impersonally unified in the Trinity Ultimate. All divine activity on the absonite level is power-personalized in God the Ultimate and impersonally unified in the Trinity Absolute.
w13.143: 4. Synthesis on the Finite Level: the Supreme Being (orig. pp. 455–461)
w13.145: Before Supremacy there is no experiential Trinity. The Supreme Being Himself is to be a member of the first experiential Trinity, so that Trinity cannot become factual until His growth is complete. Nor can the Paradise Trinity "unify" anew in order to experientialize the Supreme, since it is already, and always, absolutely unified. What the Paradise Trinity in fact did was bring forth the spirit person of God the Supreme, and this spirit person becomes the volitional focus of the entire finite power-personality unification.
w13.146: What, then, causes the Supreme to grow? The interaction of the three groups within God the Sevenfold: the Supreme Creators, the Supreme Being, and the Paradise Deities. The successes the creators achieve in time and space are gathered into the power of the Almighty, and that power unites with the spirit personality in Havona.
w13.148: Sadler notes that this union occurs on the pilot world of the outer Havona circuit, and that its medium is the Supreme Mind, derived from the Infinite Spirit. If in eternity mind "co-ordinated" the Son and Paradise, in time mind "synthesizes" power and personality.
w13.150: Yet God the Sevenfold is not merely an association. It also has other phases unrelated to spiritual and personal progress, and every one of them is to find unity in the Supreme [106:1.4]. Sadler cites the Seven Master Controllers and the "mind phase" of God the Sevenfold that he conjectured in Appendix XII. His picture is of many streams converging on the spirit person of the Supreme: from the Creator Sons, from the physical controllers, and perhaps along a path of mind that runs through the Creative Spirits and the Master Spirits to Majeston.
w13.151: The result is a new relationship between pattern and person.
w13.153: The Isle of Paradise is the absolute mechanism, and the Eternal Son is the absolute person. The two are co-ordinated by the mind of the Conjoint Actor but never became one. Within an experiential Deity, however, matter, mind, and spirit are all being joined with personality. What was not accomplished in eternity is taking place in time.
w13.154: The divergence of energies and the Supreme's share
w13.155: Sadler connects this synthesis with the "divergence" of the three energies. On Paradise, spirit and monota differ only in name; in Havona they are distinct yet harmonious. In the seven superuniverses a wide gap opens between cosmic energy and divine spirit [116:6.7]. That gap produces countless problems and disharmonies, and those problems become opportunities for creatures and creators alike to build up experience in harmonization. The greater the challenge, the greater the growth.
w13.156: The Supreme Being is not merely on the receiving end of this process.
w13.158: He is now filling experientially the potential, associative, and creative levels that Paradise Deity fills existentially.
w13.159: 5. Paradise Divinity Enriches Experiential Reality (orig. pp. 462–465)
w13.160: Next we look at the "spirit person" descending from above. Both the Supreme and the Ultimate have an origin in time, and both begin as spiritual beings in Havona. God the Supreme originates in the Paradise Trinity, and the Ultimate too is present in Havona in an absonite and superpersonal sense [106:4.3]. Sadler infers that what the Trinity does for the Supreme on the finite level it also does for the Ultimate on the absonite level. The Trinity is both the source of the two experiential Deities and the reality of absolute stability that undergirds their evolution.
w13.161: Sadler also views the sevenfold not only as a descending ladder but as a "lateral diversification." Existential Deity, once single, branches into the Seven Master Spirits (divergence) and then gathers again in the Supreme Being (convergence) to form a new unity, an experiential Deity; this is the divergence-convergence principle of Appendix XIV. Neither the Supreme nor the Ultimate is therefore the Trinity itself; each is a reflection of the Trinity's unity on its own level.
w13.163: This enrichment does not happen on Deity levels alone. Paradise divinity flows down, attenuated and diluted, so that it can be grasped on relative levels as well. The bestowals of a Creator Son unite creator and creature experientially, and the Adjuster fuses existential divinity with experiential humanity. The text compares the Adjuster's relation to man with the Trinity's relation to the Supreme.
w13.165: When a human being fuses with an Adjuster, when a Creator Son becomes like his own creatures, when the Supreme and the Ultimate power-personalize, one principle is at work on different levels. Spiritual growth within us is a small mirror of the cosmic power-personality synthesis.
w13.166: 6. Synthesis on the Absonite Level: God the Ultimate (orig. pp. 466–473)
w13.167: Before the emergence of the Supreme
w13.168: Before Supremacy emerges, the master universe is governed existentially by the Trinity of Ultimacy, while experientially its oversight is divided among four.
w13.170: The experiential Deity of this period is "prepersonal," and the Father, Son, and Spirit co-operate with Him not personally but as the Trinity [10:7.3]. Meanwhile the Master Architects, a corps complete from the beginning, administer the whole master universe in advance.
w13.171: After the emergence of the Supreme
w13.172: Once the Supreme Being has emerged, four new factors enter the absonite level. First, the Trinity Ultimate can take shape as a factual reality. Second, the Supreme Being begins a third phase of function, as a post-finite Deity, in outer space. Third, the corps of Supreme Creators, as unified Deity, qualifies for membership in the Trinity Ultimate; the text likens the factualization of the Almighty Supreme to the appearance of the Conjoint Actor in eternity [116:2.14]. Fourth, the creatures who took part in the growth of the Supreme shed their finite limits and set out on a new adventure on the absonite level.
w13.173: Sadler also brings back his conjecture from Appendix XII that in outer space God the Sevenfold may expand into God the Tenfold. The text says only that the function of God the Sevenfold will "probably be extended" in relation to outer space [0:8.12]. Sadler's God the Tenfold includes new creators such as the Son-Spirit Creative Trio, the completed Supreme Being, and the emerging Ultimate; it differs from God the Sevenfold in drawing not only on existential Paradise Deity but also on the experiential co-ordination that the finished Supreme Being provides.
w13.174: The Ultimate and the Supreme meet within the Trinity Ultimate, the Trinity Absolute, and God the Tenfold, and the two Deities also form a direct relationship with each other. That direct relationship foreshadows the Supreme-Ultimate. Sadler regards the Supreme Being as the link in all the experiential relationships of God the Ultimate.
w13.175: The Trinity Ultimate factualizes the Ultimate
w13.176: Something entirely new happens here: an experiential Deity power-personalizes because an experiential Trinity has become unified.
w13.178: The Supreme grew without an experiential Trinity, through the interaction of God the Sevenfold. The Ultimate emerges through an experiential Trinity. Their emergence therefore cannot follow the same pattern. They do share something, however. The power-personalization of the Ultimate also embraces, along with what is personal and spiritual, what is other-than-personal and nonspiritual, though over the far wider range of the entire master universe. The text itself cautions against treating the two as the same.
w13.180: Three levels of power-personality synthesis: the higher the level, the wider the range of reality embraced, and synthesis on the absolute level remains an unending task
w13.181: 7. Synthesis on the Absolute Level (orig. pp. 473–474)
w13.182: If the completion of the Supreme lifts creatures onto the absonite level, the completion of the Ultimate will open a new destiny beyond the absonite. Once the power-personalization of the Ultimate is finished, the Trinity Absolute can form as a factual reality. Sadler regards its full unification, however, as highly doubtful and perhaps impossible.
w13.183: The range of synthesis has widened at each level. The Supreme Being embraces the whole of the finite in the grand universe; the Ultimate embraces all the absonite potential of the master universe. If the Trinity Absolute could be fully unified, God the Absolute would be power-personalized from the prepersonal potential of the Deity Absolute; yet even He could not be separated from other-than-personal values either, and those point directly to the Unqualified Absolute.
w13.185: The final power-personality synthesis, then, is an attempt to achieve experientially the unity of the Absolutes that already exists existentially in eternity. It is a task with no end, no limit, and no outside. To draw out all of infinity one would have to reach the end of eternity, and eternity is as endless as infinity. Sadler asks whether the very notion of an "end" may be a habit of thought bound to time and space. Not even the Paradise Trinity can experientialize the Deity Absolute, because, though infinite, it is not an experiential Trinity.
w13.188: A few of Sadler's references contain numbering errors. The "103:8.10" he cites for another aspect of the Trinity Ultimate should be 106:8.10; the "112:8.14" given for the relation of the three energies is, judging by the page, 12:8.14; and the "110:1.5" cited for the mind phase of the Supreme is 116:1.5. Further, the contrast in which the actual side stops at co-ordination while the potential side is synthesized, the "mind phase" of God the Sevenfold, and God the Tenfold are all Sadler's interpretations, drawn together from many passages. What the text itself says goes only as far as this: the experiential Deities power-personalize, and in the process impersonal phases are being unified.
w13.189: Power-personality synthesis is the process of joining organized energy (physical, mental, and spiritual) with personality; it is the principle by which the experiential Deities grow.
w13.190: In eternity the potential side was synthesized in the Universal Absolute, while the actual side went no further than the co-ordination of mind. Sadler interprets the unification of all actual reality as a task left to the experiential Deities.
w13.191: The Supreme grows without an experiential Trinity, through the interaction of God the Sevenfold, as almighty power and spirit personality unite through the Supreme Mind.
w13.192: Within an experiential Deity even impersonal phases are being unified with personality, giving rise to a "new relationship between pattern and person."
w13.193: The Ultimate power-personalizes once the Trinity Ultimate has been unified, and is not merely an amplification of the Supreme.
w13.194: Synthesis on the absolute level is the endless task of achieving experientially a unity that already exists existentially.
w13.196: Appendix XXIII, The Trinity of Trinities (pp. 475–484)
w13.197: In the far future of the post-ultimate age the Trinity of Trinities appears and begins to gather the whole of existential and experiential Deity into one again. Sadler examines the principle by which Trinities arise and reviews the three member Trinities, then depicts the process of formation in four stages. At the end of it he arrives at a picture in which the Infinite stands both at the causal end and at the destiny end of eternity.
w13.198: 1. The Eternal Cycle of Deity (orig. pp. 475–476)
w13.199: Viewed as a whole, from the Paradise Trinity of the eternal past to the Trinity of Trinities of the remote future, the history of Deity feels like a single cycle. The revelation itself invites us to picture total reality as an ellipse.
w13.201: Sadler states the principle by which a Trinity arises. Whenever three Deities function in relation to one another on the same level of reality, a Trinity eventuates. Two make a relationship, but three make a system, and a Trinity is exactly such a system. The eternal Father, Son, and Spirit constitute the Paradise Trinity; the Supreme Being, the corps of Architects, and the corps of Supreme Creators constitute the Trinity Ultimate; and the Ultimate, joining with the Supreme and the Consummator of Universe Destiny, constitutes the Trinity Absolute.
w13.202: A Trinity is itself Deity, so it too seeks new expression. When three Trinities enter into functional relationship, a "system of systems" results: the Trinity of Trinities. It is where existential and experiential Deity are brought together once more.
w13.203: 2. An Inventory of the Three Trinities (orig. pp. 477–479)
w13.204: The revelation introduces the Trinity of Trinities as a postulate of philosophers.
w13.206: Sadler held that an experiential Trinity passes through three phases: limited, then factual, then unified (see Appendix XIX). For the Trinity of Trinities to become a factual reality, its three member Trinities must first become factual. The Trinity Ultimate becomes factual at the end of the present age and the Trinity Absolute at the end of the sixth age, so the multiple Trinity can take form only after the sixth age.
w13.207: In quality, the three Trinities differ greatly.
w13.208: The character of the three Trinities (Sadler's summary)
w13.213: The Trinity Absolute is in an especially hard position. Its function is totally absolute and its goal quantitatively infinite, yet it is itself subinfinite. The text also says that this Trinity cannot readily be classified [106:6.5]. Achieving its whole goal would mean drawing out all of infinity, so full unification would be possible only at the end of eternity. Sadler calls this a kind of deadlock.
w13.214: 3. The Stage of Incompletion and the Trinitization of the Supreme-Ultimate (orig. pp. 479–480)
w13.215: Following the structure of 106:8, Sadler sees the Trinity of Trinities in three tiers. The first level is the three Trinities; the second is the association of the Supreme, the Ultimate, and "the Absolute"; and the third lies above them.
w13.217: The first level forms without difficulty. The obstacle lies on the second. The Supreme and the Ultimate are present, but because the Trinity Absolute cannot unify, God the Absolute has not emerged. The existential and potential Deity Absolute cannot take its place beside experiential Deities. Sadler calls this condition "Stage One: the stage of incompletion." If the infinite Paradise Trinity makes up for what is missing, the structure can function, but not in a mature way.
w13.218: To break the deadlock, Sadler fastens on a passage in the text.
w13.220: The Paradise Trinity came into being through the Father and the Son's trinitizing of the Conjoint Actor. By analogy, what would follow if the Supreme and the Ultimate were to trinitize together? The two are subinfinite but probably coabsolute Deities, so the outcome would likewise be limited in universality of reality yet absolute in quality of being. Sadler calls this being "the trinitized expression of God the Absolute," or the Limited-Absolute. The name is Sadler's and does not appear in the text.
w13.221: 4. The Stage of Initial Factuality and the Stage of Growing Unification (orig. pp. 481–483)
w13.222: When the Limited-Absolute appears, the second level is filled, but in an initial sense rather than a final one, because the Limited-Absolute gathers a meaningful portion of the potentials of the Deity Absolute, not all of them. At this point, Sadler says, the best concept is to place the Universal Absolute on the third level. This is "Stage Two: the stage of initial factuality." In Sadler's image, a beachhead has been secured on the shore of infinity, yet the embrace of infinity is still very far off.
w13.223: Sadler's picture of the three levels of the Trinity of Trinities and the stages of its formation; who occupies the second and third levels changes from stage to stage
w13.224: In "Stage Three: the stage of growing unification" the Trinity Absolute goes on unifying, and God the Absolute, now emerged, takes part in His own growth "personally," unlike the two Deities before Him. Because the second level is itself an association of three experiential Deities, it seeks unification as a Trinity (the "third experiential Trinity" of Appendix XXIV), and the whole multiple Trinity grows toward unity.
w13.225: Yet the three Absolutes are infinite and can never be exhausted. However much growth occurs, most of them remain outside the multiple Trinity. The place on the third level therefore still belongs to the Universal Absolute. Here Sadler recalls the view of a Universal Censor.
w13.227: Sadler emphasizes that this is not a deadlock but a dynamic situation of endless growth.
w13.228: 5. The Stage of Hypothetical Completion (orig. pp. 483–484)
w13.229: Finally, Sadler simply supposes. What if the Trinity of Trinities were completely unified in the total sense? The first level would hold three fully unified Trinities, and the second the association of the Supreme, the Ultimate, and the Absolute, an Absolute with no qualification whatever. If the three Absolutes, existentially one, became one experientially as well and filled the second level, who would then occupy the third?
w13.230: For comparison, Sadler looks back to the other end of eternity. The revelation depicts a "hypothetical static moment" of the eternal past.
w13.232: Sadler calls the end of future eternity a "hypothetical static-dynamic moment." Every potential would have been infinitely experientialized and exhausted, so the dynamics of creation, evolution, eventuation, and supercreation would at last come to rest. Nothing would remain to be done. At that moment the third level would hold not the Universal Absolute but the Infinite. The Infinite met at the causal end would be met again at the destiny end.
w13.233: But Sadler insists that this holds good conceptually only; as an actuality it remains eternally remote. In terms of the ellipse, the curve bends back toward its point of departure but never closes. The appendix ends with a brief saying of a Universal Censor.
w13.236: The revelation speaks of the structure of the Trinity of Trinities (three levels), of the deitization of Majeston as a manifestation of the second-level association [106:8.20], and of the appearance of the Supreme-Ultimate and the possible trinitization of God the Absolute [0:12.8]. The division into four stages, the name Limited-Absolute, the "static-dynamic moment" of future eternity, and the placing of the Universal Absolute and the Infinite on the third level are all Sadler's inferences.
w13.237: When three Deities relating on one level form a "system," a Trinity eventuates; when three Trinities form a system, the result is the Trinity of Trinities.
w13.238: It can take form as a factual reality only after the sixth age.
w13.239: The Trinity Absolute is experiential, absolute, and subinfinite, and since it cannot be fully unified it stands in a deadlock.
w13.240: In Sadler's view the deadlock is broken by a trinitization of God the Absolute on the part of the Supreme-Ultimate, from which the Limited-Absolute appears.
w13.241: The formation is pictured in four stages: incompletion, initial factuality, growing unification, and hypothetical completion. The last is possible only as a concept.
